origin_region: Yunnan · Dali · Xiaguan (leaf from Lincang, Baoshan, Pu'er and Xishuangbanna)
cultivar: Blended Yunnan large-leaf plantation and arbor leaf from several prefectures
processing: Raw pu-erh maocha, blended across regions and grades, steamed, pressed very tightly into a 100 g or 250 g bowl-shaped nest with a hollow underneath, and oven- or air-dried; Xiaguan's drying traditionally leaves a light smoky note.
harvest_season: Blended from spring, summer and autumn maocha and released by production year rather than by harvest.
appearance_dry: A dense, hard, grey-green to brown nest with a smooth domed top, a dimple underneath and small buds pressed flat into the surface.
appearance_liquor: Bright yellow-orange when young, deep amber to red after a decade, clear once the rinse has cleared the dust.
appearance_wet: Small to medium chopped leaves, uniform in grade, that take two or three steeps to loosen from the core.
taste_profile: Sharp and bracing when young, with a dry smokiness, a firm bitterness, mineral and pine notes and a quick sweetness; with ten or more years it turns plummy, woody and surprisingly deep for the price.

brewing.notes: Rinse twice with boiling water; the second rinse can be 15–20 seconds to loosen the chunks. Break the tuo from the dimple side with a pick into layered pieces, not powder. Boiling water throughout; a clay pot takes the edge off the smoke.

vintage_note: Sold by production year and grade, with the Jia Ji (grade A, green box), Te Ji (special grade) and Cang Er tuo as the long-running sheng lines, and by special series for Taiwanese and Hong Kong distributors (the FT and similar editions) that collectors track by year. Young (1–5 years) Xiaguan tuo is harsh and smoky and is bought cheaply to put away; the 8–20-year window is where it shines, and 1990s and early-2000s tuo are among the most affordable genuinely aged sheng available, partly because tight pressing and Dali's dry air slow the ageing down. Current supply spans roughly 1995–2025 in large quantity, with dry Kunming or Dali storage the norm and Guangdong-stored examples softer and darker.
description:
Xiaguan tuo is the nest-shaped pu-erh from the Xiaguan Tea Factory in Dali, a plant founded in 1941 (as the Kangzang Tea Factory) that became the great tuo specialist of Yunnan; the bowl-with-a-dimple shape itself is usually credited to Dali merchants in the early 1900s, designed to travel well along the trade routes to Sichuan and Tibet. For generations it was the everyday pu-erh of south-west China, and it is still the cheapest way to buy honest tea that ages.

The factory blends maocha from several prefectures (Lincang, Baoshan, Pu'er, Xishuangbanna) by grade rather than by village, steams it and presses it under heavy pressure into 100 g or 250 g nests. The signature smoky note comes from the factory's traditional drying and handling, not from added smoke, and it fades with age into something more like pine and dried plum.

Young, a Xiaguan tuo is bracing: bitter, dry, smoky, mineral, with a short sweetness, and it is not a tea to charm a beginner. Ten years on, especially in slightly humid storage, it becomes plummy, woody and deep, and people who dismissed it come back to it. Brew it with boiling water, two rinses and a pick: breaking the nest into clean layers rather than powder is the whole skill.

It is sold by production year and grade, with the Jia Ji green-box tuo the classic, Te Ji and Cang Er a step up, and a bewildering run of special editions for Taiwanese and Hong Kong dealers that collectors trade by year and wrapper. Prices are low for new tuo and still reasonable for twenty-year-old ones, which makes them the standard recommendation for learning what aged sheng tastes like without spending a fortune. The factory also makes shu tuo and tight 'Tibetan' mushroom-shaped jincha, so check the box says sheng.

Buy a few of the same year, drink one now, and open the next every five years; it is the cheapest education in ageing that pu-erh offers.
sources_note: The 1941 founding as Kangzang Tea Factory is from company history; the attribution of the tuo shape to Dali merchants (the Yongchang Xiang firm, around 1902) is the standard account but rests on trade histories rather than primary records.
